title: node-electrostatic-hypothesis-log-2029-12-05
content:
Summary:

This doc captures a working hypothesis and stepped investigation plan that the recent cluster-level ECC spikes and intermittent NVLink negotiation loops may be precipitated by transient electrical noise (electrostatic discharge, power rail ripple, or grounding anomalies) rather than a single faulty driver or model of card. We describe observed signals, why ESD/power ripple is plausible, immediate mitigations for on-call, and a set of lab and fleet experiments to validate or falsify this hypothesis.

Context / Why this is different from prior notes:
- Most prior work focused on firmware/driver regressions, thermal throttling, and persistent hardware defects. This file intentionally explores transient electrical/environmental vectors (ESD, ground loops, PSU ripple, rack PDU misconfiguration) that could produce bursts of correctable ECC followed by link flaps and occasional kernel oops.
- We are treating this as a system-level phenomenon that can simultaneously affect NVLink negotiation and ECC reporting on multiple cards in one rack or adjacent racks.

High-level timeline of a representative incident (2029-11-30 02:14 UTC):
- 02:12:33 UTC: kubelet reports pod failures on node gpu-rack12-07.
- 02:12:40 UTC: telemetry shows 1.4k/sec burst of corrected ECC on gpu0 and gpu1 for ~18s.
- 02:12:45 UTC: NVLink negotiation error (link down/up) observed for gpulink1 on both devices.
- 02:12:58 UTC: kernel oops on gpu driver, stacktrace signature root=nvlink_negotiation.c:485.
- 02:13:05 UTC: node became unresponsive for ~45s and entered kernel watchdog reset.
- 02:15:30 UTC: node came back; many pods re-scheduled.

Observed signals (aggregated across 6 incidents sharing pattern):
- Short-lived bursts of correctable ECC (correctable counters spike up to thousands over 10-40s then decay).
- NVLink link-down / negotiation-loop events correlated within seconds of ECC bursts.
- Occasional single-card kernel panic or driver oops; not always the same card model.
- Events cluster by rack and adjacent PDUs rather than by card serial or batch.
- No clear software update or driver rollouts coincident with incidents.
- IPMI / BMC logs sometimes show small voltage dips on 12V rail within the same second range.
- Ambient temperature and thermal sensors normal for the period.

Why electrical transients / ESD / power ripple is plausible:
- ECC bursts are an immediate artifact of single-event upsets and transient particle/noise events. Sustained manufacturing defects usually produce persistent ECC increases rather than short, synchronized bursts across multiple GPUs.
- NVLink negotiation is sensitive to link signal integrity; a short electrical glitch can cause link retraining.
- Kernel oops stack traces often point to the driver being handed corrupted state; transient noise could flip bits in the GPU or in interconnect buffers, causing inconsistent sanity checks.
- Rack-level clustering of incidents suggests a shared infrastructure root (PDU, bus, ground) rather than isolated cards.

Immediate on-call mitigations (quick playbook for next alert):
1) Quarantine the node(s): cordon + drain with live-migration/pod-eviction. Command: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
2) Snapshot telemetry window (retain debug-level logs):
   - nvml/nvidia-smi logs, dmesg, journalctl -k, ipmi sensor logs, BMC event logs.
   - Suggested commands: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,serial,driver_model,temperature.gpu,voltage --format=csv; journalctl -k -S "2029-11-30 02:10" -U "2029-11-30 02:20" > /tmp/kernel-window.log
3) If multiple nodes in a rack show correlated events, power-cycle the PDU feed for that rack on a controlled schedule (working with data center ops). Avoid single-card swaps until we validate PSU behavior.
4) Temporarily enforce model fallback routing: redirect latency-sensitive routes away from impacted racks for 2–6 hours.
5) Create high-priority incident ticket with links to collected artifacts and tag SRE-hardware and infra-ops.

Forensics checklist (what to collect before rebooting / re-provisioning):
- /var/log/journal window covering before-during-after window.
- dmesg output and kernel oops logs.
- nvidia-smi -q (per device) and nvlink state.
- ipmitool sensor list and sel list output; BMC SEL timestamps.
- PDU logs (voltage/current time-series) for the rack.
- Cabling photos and rack grounding strap inspection note.
- PCIe/slot occupancy and lspci -vvv for link training info.
- Onboard tracing if available (driver debug traces).

Hypotheses ranked (quick):
A) Transient power rail ripple on 12V or auxiliary rails causing ECC flips and NVLink retraining (priority: high).
B) Ground loop or missing earth bond causing ESD like discharges in bursts across a rack (priority: medium-high).
C) Firmware/driver-issued DMA corruption coincidentally exposing memory errors (priority: medium).
D) Bad batch of GPU hardware or midplane cable intermittency (priority: medium).
E) Cosmic/ionizing particle events producing single-event upsets (low probability given clustering by rack).

Planned lab experiments (owners assigned):
- Controlled power injection test (Diego Ramos): replicate rack PSU behavior by injecting low-amplitude ripple on 12V rails while running memtest and NVLink stress for 1h. Capture ECC counters. Target date: 2029-12-10.
- Ground-lift simulation (Marcus Liu): temporarily change ground bonding in isolated rack emulation to observe how link retrain frequency responds; use ESD simulator to generate calibrated discharges to chassis. Target: 2029-12-12.
- Cross-driver validation (Sofia Chen): boot same card firmware with two driver versions and run synthetic NVLink stress; check for divergence in error rates. Target: 2029-12-08.
- PDU telemetry replay (Aisha Patel): replay logged PDU voltage waveforms into a lab power supply and correlate with ECC spike reproduction. Target: 2029-12-11.

Fleet-level actions to test hypothesis without risking too many nodes:
- Install ephemeral ipmi/pdu voltage sampling hook in suspect racks to increase sampling rate during off-hours for two weeks.
- Add temporary alert: "rack_ecc_burst_v2" when corrected_ecc_rate > baseline*10 AND nvlink_link_retrain_count > 3 within 30s.
- During maintenance windows, swap pdu feed to alternative UPS branch for one rack and observe.

Telemetry queries (examples to run immediately):
- PromQL (ECC bursts): sum by(node) (increase(gpu_ecc_corrected_total[1m])) > 1000
- NVLink retrain count: increase(gpu_nvlink_retrain_total[1m]) > 3
- Join on host metadata to find co-occurrence with ipmi_voltage_12v: increase(ipmi_voltage_12v_dips_total[1m]) > 0

Driver / kernel fingerprints to look for in collected logs:
- nvlink_negotiation.c: stack frames around "link_retrain_request" and "link_error_count"
- nvidia kernel oops with register dumps showing single-bit flips in VRAM address ranges near runtime heaps.

Safety and escalation guidance for on-call:
- If we observe repeated kernel panics on multiple nodes in same rack within 24 hours, escalate to infra-ops and schedule a rack-level maintenance window.
- Do NOT proceed to swap GPUs across racks until PSU/power-cable and grounding checks are completed; swapping could spread the fault or mask if it is rack-level.

Open questions to prioritize in experiments:
- Can we reproduce ECC bursts by injecting <100mV ripple on the 12V rail while under NVLink load? (If yes -> power-hardware root cause likely).
- Do ECC bursts always precede NVLink retraining, or can NVLink flaps occur first? Order matters for causal inference.
- Are there any non-GPU devices in the same PDUs showing correlated voltage dips (TPUs, NICs)?
- Are there maintenance activities or intermittent rack personnel touching racks at correlated times (human ESD source)?

Next steps (action items with owners):
- Aisha: gather PDU logs for the 6 incidents and produce a merged time-aligned CSV. Due 2029-12-07.
- Diego: stand up lab rig for controlled ripple injection and run first replication test. Due 2029-12-10.
- Marcus: coordinate on-site grounding inspection with dc-ops for rack12 and adjacent racks. Due 2029-12-09.
- Sofia: prepare kernel + driver boot images for cross-driver validation; schedule 2-hour test runs. Due 2029-12-08.

Notes / working hypotheses addenda:
- If lab tests are inconclusive, consider high-resolution logic capture on NVLink lanes (requires specialized probes) to see if bit errors are present on the physical link. This is expensive but may be necessary if waveform evidence is ambiguous.
- We should consider modifying alerts to include "rack-affinity" so future incidents are grouped by rack PDU rather than by model or serial to help detect infrastructure-level faults sooner.

Appendix: Common commands and snippets for evidence capture
- nvidia-smi -q -x > /tmp/gpu-q.xml
- journalctl -k -S "2029-11-30 02:10" -U "2029-11-30 02:20" > /tmp/journal-window.log
- ipmitool sensor list > /tmp/ipmi-sensors.txt; ipmitool sel list > /tmp/ipmi-sel.txt
- cat /sys/class/drm/card*/device/nvlink_state* (if present)
- lspci -vvv | grep -A4 "NVIDIA" > /tmp/lspci-nvidia.txt

If you are reading this as a reviewer: this is intentionally exploratory and high-level; tests should be repro'd in lab before broad fleet changes. Please add any data correlations or prior incidents that support or contradict the electrical transient hypothesis.
